title: Stopping the harm before trial
subtitle: The American Cyanamid framework for interim injunctions
objectives: State the three stages of the American Cyanamid test for a prohibitory interim injunction
Explain why a mandatory interim injunction is held to a materially higher threshold than a prohibitory one, and what an undertaking in damages requires of the applicant
Apply the American Cyanamid framework to a fact pattern and reach a reasoned view on whether an interim injunction is likely to be granted

leadingAuthorities.citation: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes the three-stage test for a prohibitory interim injunction: serious question to be tried, adequacy of damages, balance of convenience

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Candidates often collapse the American Cyanamid test into a single question — 'does the claimant have a good case?' — when the whole point of the test is that the merits are deliberately the weakest of the three stages. SQE1 rewards candidates who can work through all three stages in order and stop at the first one that resolves the application. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name the three stages — this lesson checks whether you can actually run through them on a fact pattern.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the bare test before. The test pool below leans on full fact patterns requiring you to work through serious question, adequacy of damages, and balance of convenience in sequence.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and fix the low threshold at stage one precisely — 'serious question to be tried' is deliberately undemanding, and treating it as a full merits assessment is the most common source of lost marks here.

overview.hook: A former employee is about to start work for a direct competitor, in apparent breach of a restrictive covenant. By the time the underlying breach-of-contract claim reaches trial in eighteen months, the damage — client relationships gone, confidential pricing leaked — will already be done. An interim injunction is the only remedy that can actually stop the harm before it happens. But courts are wary of effectively deciding a case on an early, incomplete picture of the evidence — which is exactly the tension the American Cyanamid test was built to manage.

parts.heading: Why interim injunctions exist, and why courts are cautious about granting them
parts.voice: argumentative — states the tension before resolving it
body: Most civil remedies are awarded at the end of a case, once all the evidence has been tested at trial. An interim injunction is different: it is an order made before trial, often within days or weeks of an application, to preserve a position or stop an ongoing harm while the underlying dispute is still being litigated.

That urgency creates a genuine problem. A court asked to grant an interim injunction is being asked to intervene — sometimes decisively — on the basis of witness statements and documents assembled in a hurry, without cross-examination and often without full disclosure. Get it wrong, and the court has effectively decided the case for one side long before trial, based on an incomplete picture.

House of Lords in American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd addressed this directly: rather than asking the court to form a view on who is likely to win at trial, the test asks a structured sequence of lesser questions, designed to let the court act to prevent harm without prejudging the merits it isn't yet equipped to judge.

components.definition: A court order made before trial, requiring a party to do or refrain from doing something for the duration of the proceedings (or until further order), granted to prevent harm that could not adequately be remedied once the case is finally decided.

interaction.prompt: Why did the House of Lords in American Cyanamid deliberately avoid asking the court to assess which party was likely to win at trial?
options: Because the court, at the interim stage, has an incomplete evidential picture and full assessment risks prejudging the case before trial
Because trial judges are legally required to ignore the interim court's findings regardless of their quality
Because interim injunctions are never actually necessary in practice
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the structured, lower-threshold test exists precisely because an interim hearing is not equipped to resolve contested merits properly.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The concern is evidential: at the interim stage the court has not heard cross-examined evidence or seen full disclosure, so a full merits assessment risks deciding the case prematurely on an incomplete picture.

parts.heading: Stage one: a serious question to be tried
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the case's own language outward
body: The first stage of American Cyanamid asks only whether there is a serious question to be tried — that is, whether the claim is not frivolous or vexatious, and has some real substance to it. This is a deliberately low bar. The court does not weigh the relative strength of each side's case, and it does not try to predict who would win at trial.

Lord Diplock was explicit that the claimant does not need to show a prima facie case that they will win at trial, still less a probability of success — they only need to show the claim is genuinely arguable. In practice, the great majority of applications clear this hurdle easily; it exists mainly to filter out applications with no underlying legal substance at all.

This is the stage examiners most often use to test precise recall, because it's tempting to answer with a much higher-sounding threshold ('a strong case', 'likely to succeed') that simply isn't what American Cyanamid actually requires.

components.citation: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396
components.text: The court no doubt must be satisfied that the claim is not frivolous or vexatious; in other words, that there is a serious question to be tried. It is no part of the court's function at this stage of the litigation to try to resolve conflicts of evidence on affidavit as to facts on which the claims of either party may ultimately depend, nor to decide difficult questions of law which call for detailed argument and mature considerations.
elements: The claim must not be frivolous or vexatious
A genuinely arguable claim is sufficient — no need to show likely success
The court does not resolve conflicts of evidence at this stage
The court does not decide difficult points of law requiring full argument at this stage

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows the claimant has cleared the 'serious question to be tried' threshold.
interaction.scenarioText: A claimant seeks an interim injunction to restrain an alleged breach of a non-compete clause. The clause is a standard, commercially reasonable restriction, and the claimant has produced evidence the defendant approached at least one client using confidential pricing information obtained during employment.
tappableSpans: approached at least one client using confidential pricing information
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A restriction that is not obviously unenforceable, combined with evidence of apparent breach, is enough to show the claim is genuinely arguable — that's all stage one requires.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The key fact is that the restrictive covenant itself is not obviously invalid — a 'standard, commercially reasonable restriction' is the detail showing the underlying claim is genuinely arguable, clearing the low stage-one threshold.

parts.heading: Stages two and three: adequacy of damages and the balance of convenience
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the rest of the framework
body: Once a serious question is established, the court moves to the question that usually decides the application: would damages, awarded at trial if the claimant ultimately wins, be an adequate remedy for the harm suffered in the meantime? If damages would fully compensate the claimant for any harm suffered while waiting for trial, an interim injunction is generally refused — there is no need for the court to intervene early if money will put things right later.

Where damages would not be an adequate remedy for the claimant — because the harm is not readily quantifiable, involves loss of reputation, disclosure of genuinely confidential information, or the collapse of a business — the court asks the same question in reverse: would damages under the claimant's undertaking be an adequate remedy for the defendant, if it turns out the injunction should not have been granted? If both are inadequate, or the adequacy of damages doesn't clearly favour either side, the court moves to the balance of convenience.

The balance of convenience is a broad, practical weighing exercise: which course — granting or refusing the injunction — carries the lower risk of injustice, taking into account matters such as maintaining the status quo, the relative strength of each party's case where it is otherwise unclear (a genuine tie-breaker, used sparingly), and any other relevant practical factor. Where everything else is finely balanced, the court will generally lean towards preserving the status quo pending trial.

components.label: The three American Cyanamid stages
points: Stage 1: Is there a serious question to be tried? (A low threshold — not frivolous or vexatious, genuinely arguable)
Stage 2: Would damages be an adequate remedy for the claimant if refused, or for the defendant (under the claimant's undertaking) if granted?
Stage 3: If damages are inadequate on both sides, where does the balance of convenience lie? (status quo, relative strength of the case as a last resort, other practical factors)

interaction.prompt: Put the American Cyanamid stages in the order the court works through them.
items: Adequacy of damages as a remedy
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: a low-threshold merits filter first, then the decisive adequacy-of-damages question, and only if that doesn't resolve things, a broader balance of convenience.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The order matters because each stage is only reached if the previous one doesn't resolve the application: serious question first, then adequacy of damages, and balance of convenience only as a final tie-breaker.

parts.heading: Mandatory injunctions: a genuinely higher bar
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the distinction before resolving it
body: Everything so far describes a prohibitory injunction — an order restraining a defendant from doing something. What about a mandatory interim injunction, ordering a defendant to positively do something (reinstate a supply contract, demolish an unlawful structure, restore removed goods) before trial?

Courts treat mandatory interim injunctions with materially more caution than prohibitory ones, because compelling positive action before trial is a more intrusive and often less reversible step than simply freezing a situation. The test applied is stricter than the ordinary serious-question threshold: the court generally requires the applicant to show a high degree of assurance that they would succeed at trial — sometimes expressed as needing a strong prima facie case — not merely an arguable one.

This distinction is a favourite SQE1 trap: a fact pattern that superficially looks like an ordinary American Cyanamid case can actually be asking for mandatory relief, and answering with the ordinary 'serious question' threshold when the higher mandatory threshold applies is a common and costly error.

components.title: Prohibitory or mandatory: which threshold applies?
components.description: A decision path for identifying which threshold governs an interim injunction application.

nodes.label: Does the order sought require the defendant to positively do something, rather than refrain from something?
Yes — mandatory injunction: apply the stricter, higher threshold (a high degree of assurance of success at trial)
No — prohibitory injunction: apply the ordinary American Cyanamid three-stage test

components.textAlternative: First identify whether the order sought is mandatory (requiring positive action) or prohibitory (requiring restraint). A mandatory interim injunction is held to a stricter threshold requiring a high degree of assurance of success at trial. A prohibitory injunction is assessed under the ordinary three-stage American Cyanamid test.

interaction.prompt: A claimant applies for an interim order requiring the defendant to immediately reconnect a utility supply it disconnected in alleged breach of contract. What threshold governs this application?
options: The ordinary 'serious question to be tried' threshold, because any American Cyanamid case uses the same test
The stricter mandatory injunction threshold, because the order compels positive action rather than restraining conduct
No threshold applies, because utility disputes are excluded from injunctive relief
The criminal standard of proof, because disconnection is treated as a public law matter
interaction.trapExplanation: The trap is applying the default prohibitory test without noticing the order sought is mandatory — reconnecting a supply compels positive action, which triggers the stricter threshold requiring a high degree of assurance of success at trial, not the ordinary serious-question standard.

parts.heading: The price of an interim injunction: the undertaking in damages
parts.voice: reflective — closes by tying the framework to its practical cost
body: An interim injunction is never granted for free. As a near-universal condition, the applicant must give the court a cross-undertaking in damages: a formal promise to compensate the respondent for any loss caused by the injunction, if it later turns out at trial that the injunction should not have been granted.

This matters for two reasons this module will keep returning to. First, it's the mechanism that makes the adequacy-of-damages question at stage two symmetrical — the court isn't just protecting the claimant from irreparable harm, it's also protecting the defendant, because the claimant's undertaking stands behind any harm the injunction turns out to have caused unfairly. Second, it means an applicant needs to be able to satisfy the court they could actually honour the undertaking if called on — a claimant without the means to pay significant damages is a real, practical weakness in an application, quite apart from the merits.

Carry the whole framework forward as a discipline, not a checklist to recite: serious question (a low bar), then adequacy of damages (usually decisive), then balance of convenience (a last-resort tie-breaker) — with a materially stricter threshold the moment the order sought becomes mandatory rather than prohibitory.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often treat the undertaking in damages as a formality that doesn't affect the substance of whether an injunction is granted.
components.whyItsWrong: The undertaking is doing real work in the test itself: it is precisely what makes the adequacy-of-damages question at stage two symmetrical, since it's what the defendant would recover against if the injunction turns out to have been wrongly granted. A claimant who could not honour the undertaking presents a genuine weakness the court will weigh, not a mere paperwork step.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that an applicant for an interim injunction must promise to compensate the respondent if the injunction later turns out to have been wrongly granted?
sliderLabels: Not confident — no such promise is required
Confident — the cross-undertaking in damages is a near-universal condition
interaction.correctPosition: Confident — the cross-undertaking in damages is a near-universal condition
interaction.explanation: Correct. As a near-universal condition of interim relief, the applicant gives a cross-undertaking in damages, compensating the respondent for loss caused by the injunction if it is later found to have been wrongly granted.

testPool.prompt: What must a claimant show to satisfy the first American Cyanamid stage?
options: A serious question to be tried — a genuinely arguable claim that is not frivolous or vexatious
A probability of success at trial exceeding 50%
A cast-iron case with no realistic defence available
That the defendant has already admitted liability

testPool.prompt: What is a cross-undertaking in damages?
options: A promise by the applicant to compensate the respondent for loss caused by the injunction if it is later found to have been wrongly granted
A promise by the respondent to comply with the injunction without objection
A statutory cap on the damages recoverable at trial
A form of security for costs unique to injunction applications

testPool.prompt: A junior lawyer says the American Cyanamid test requires the court to decide which party is more likely to win at trial. Is this correct?
options: No — the test deliberately avoids assessing the relative merits, asking instead only whether a serious question exists, before turning to adequacy of damages and balance of convenience
Yes — assessing who is likely to win is exactly what stage one requires
Yes, but only for claims valued above £100,000
No — the test is entirely unrelated to the merits of the underlying claim at any stage

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three American Cyanamid stages?
options: Serious question to be tried
Adequacy of damages as a remedy
Balance of convenience
Proof beyond reasonable doubt that the claim will succeed
testPool.trapExplanation: 'Proof beyond reasonable doubt' is a criminal standard that has no place in civil interim relief, and American Cyanamid explicitly rejects requiring even a civil probability of success at stage one — the real three stages are serious question, adequacy of damages, and balance of convenience.

testPool.prompt: A claimant argues damages would clearly be an adequate remedy for any harm it suffers while waiting for trial. What is the likely effect of this on an application for a prohibitory interim injunction?
options: The application is likely to be refused, since adequate damages generally remove the need for early intervention
The application is likely to be granted automatically once a serious question is shown
It is irrelevant — adequacy of damages is only considered for mandatory injunctions
The court will grant the injunction but reduce the cross-undertaking in damages to zero
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming clearing stage one (serious question) is enough to succeed. If damages would adequately compensate the claimant for any interim harm, that usually resolves the application in the defendant's favour at stage two, regardless of how the first stage went.

testPool.prompt: A claimant seeks to restrain a defendant from disclosing genuinely confidential trade secrets to a competitor. The claimant argues that, once disclosed, the confidentiality is destroyed forever and no sum of money could restore it. How does this argument fit into the American Cyanamid framework?
options: It supports a finding that damages would not be an adequate remedy for the claimant, pointing towards stage two favouring an injunction
It is irrelevant, because confidentiality claims are assessed under a wholly separate test
It automatically satisfies stage one and ends the analysis without considering damages
It only becomes relevant if the injunction sought is mandatory rather than prohibitory
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is treating this as satisfying the whole test or as irrelevant. It is squarely a stage-two point: irreversible harm that money cannot undo is the classic case for finding damages inadequate for the claimant, which is what pushes the analysis towards granting the injunction (subject to weighing the defendant's position too).

testPool.prompt: A claimant applies for a prohibitory interim injunction to stop a defendant using allegedly infringing branding pending trial. The claim is genuinely arguable, the claimant would suffer reputational harm that is difficult to quantify if the branding continues, and the defendant would suffer only readily quantifiable lost sales if restrained and later vindicated at trial. What is the likely outcome?
options: An injunction is likely to be granted, since damages are inadequate for the claimant's reputational harm but adequate for the defendant's quantifiable losses under the undertaking
The application fails outright at stage one because branding disputes are not 'serious questions'
The application must fail because the defendant would suffer any loss at all
The court will refuse to consider damages at all in a branding dispute
testPool.explanation: With a serious question established, the case turns on stage two: reputational harm that's hard to quantify makes damages inadequate for the claimant, while the defendant's losses (quantifiable lost sales) are adequately covered by the claimant's cross-undertaking — a combination that typically favours granting the injunction.

testPool.prompt: A claimant seeks an interim injunction ordering a defendant to demolish a wall built in alleged breach of a boundary agreement, before the underlying trespass claim is heard. Which threshold should the claimant expect to have to meet?
options: A stricter threshold than the ordinary serious-question test, because demolishing the wall is a mandatory order compelling positive action
The ordinary serious-question threshold, since all interim injunctions are assessed identically
No threshold at all, since boundary disputes are excluded from interim relief
A lower threshold than usual, because building disputes are treated leniently
testPool.explanation: An order to demolish something is mandatory — it compels positive action rather than restraining conduct — so the stricter mandatory injunction threshold applies, requiring a high degree of assurance of success at trial rather than the ordinary serious-question standard.

testPool.prompt: Which case establishes the three-stage test used for prohibitory interim injunctions?
options: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396
R v Miller [1983] 2 AC 161
Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789
Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562

testPool.prompt: According to the American Cyanamid judgment, what should the court avoid doing at the interim stage in relation to conflicting witness evidence?
options: Resolving the conflicts of evidence itself, since that is a matter for trial
Reading the witness evidence at all before the hearing
Allowing the parties to file any evidence in support of the application
Requiring the applicant to identify which witnesses it intends to call

testPool.prompt: Where the balance of convenience is otherwise finely balanced between the parties, which factor does the framework treat as a sensible practical tie-breaker?
options: Maintaining the status quo pending trial
Whichever party filed their application first in time
Whichever party has instructed leading counsel
The geographical location of the court hearing the application

testPool.prompt: A claimant cannot demonstrate it has any significant assets or means to satisfy a cross-undertaking in damages, but otherwise presents a strong case under stages one and two. What is the likely relevance of this fact to the application?
options: It is a genuine practical weakness the court will weigh, since the undertaking is meant to protect the defendant if the injunction turns out to have been wrongly granted
It is entirely irrelevant, since the undertaking is a formality with no bearing on whether relief is granted
It automatically defeats the application regardless of the merits under stages one and two
It is only relevant to mandatory injunctions, not prohibitory ones

testPool.prompt: A trainee is asked to summarise, in one sentence, why mandatory interim injunctions are treated more cautiously than prohibitory ones. Which summary is most accurate?
options: Compelling positive action before trial is a more intrusive and often less easily reversible step than simply freezing the status quo, so a higher degree of assurance of success is required
Mandatory injunctions are simply unavailable at the interim stage under any circumstances
Mandatory injunctions require a jury, unlike prohibitory injunctions
There is no meaningful difference in practice between the two thresholds
testPool.explanation: The heightened caution reflects the practical asymmetry: undoing a positive act already carried out (demolition, reinstatement) is often harder than simply lifting a restraint, so the court insists on a higher degree of assurance of trial success before compelling it.

testPool.prompt: A colleague argues that because American Cyanamid sets a low threshold at stage one, most applications for a prohibitory interim injunction succeed on the merits alone. Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: Because clearing the low stage-one threshold is only the entry point — the application is usually actually decided at stage two (adequacy of damages) or stage three (balance of convenience)
Because stage one is in fact the hardest stage to satisfy, not the easiest
Because American Cyanamid has been overruled and no longer applies to prohibitory injunctions
Because prohibitory injunctions are never granted regardless of the test applied
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is conflating a low first hurdle with a high overall success rate. Stage one filters out only hopeless claims; the practical outcome of most applications turns on stage two (or, failing that, stage three), not on how easily stage one was cleared.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'serious question to be tried' as if it were a full merits assessment, and failing to spot when a fact pattern is actually seeking a mandatory order — which triggers a materially stricter threshold than the ordinary American Cyanamid test.
